Consider the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/e1af4903eb9348ae20fc0de7ecdcbd5837257a85ae6ebd622d359c82b8719f85.svg) By evaluating the following quadratic forms at $\mathbf{x}$ **only,** determine which of them **cannot** be negative-definite.

I. $R(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2 - 3x_2^2 + 5x_1x_2$

II. ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/4d69526b89a09769a7fff19f231d31f9d6b1ac641916320fdb7483f8f2ffa9e2.svg)

III. $T(\mathbf{x})=x_2^2 + 8x_1x_2$
question.worked_solution:
A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is negative-definite if $Q(\mathbf{x}) \lt 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the quadratic forms by substituting ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/067337418c7a579839e3ec13f52df9133d2db1a8cba58971dd25704087b707a7.svg)

- Quadratic form I *might* be negative-definite. Indeed, 

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={2}^{2}-3\cdot {7}^{2}+5\cdot 2\cdot 7 \\  & =4-147+70 \\  & =-73<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Quadratic form II *cannot* be negative-definite since

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =110>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Quadratic form III *cannot* be negative-definite since

$$
\begin{aligned}T(x) & ={7}^{2}+8\cdot 2\cdot 7 \\  & =49+112 \\  & =161>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."
